Selling a home on the Gulf Coast

From pricing to closing day, here's how selling works on the Mississippi Gulf Coast, and the paperwork that helps buyers say yes faster.

After 15 years as an investor, I look at a house the way buyers, inspectors and insurers will. I'll help you put your money into the fixes that change the sale price, and have your flood, wind and roof paperwork ready before a buyer asks for it.

01

Step 1: Find out what your home is worth

Start with real sales near you and what you'll walk away with.

Online estimates are a starting point, but they can't see inside your home. A local comparison looks at recent sales of similar homes nearby, homes for sale now, and your home's condition and updates.

Ask for an estimated net sheet too. It subtracts your mortgage payoff, closing costs and other expenses from the sale price, so you can see what you'd actually take home.

02

Step 2: Gather your paperwork

On the Coast, buyers and their insurers ask for more documents.

Pull together what buyers will want to see. Having it ready can save days once you're under contract and helps buyers get insurance quotes quickly.

  • Elevation certificate, if you have one
  • Flood insurance policy and current premium
  • Homeowners and wind policy information
  • FORTIFIED roof certificate or wind mitigation report
  • Roof age, permits and warranty
  • Termite bond and inspection history
  • Receipts for major repairs and upgrades
  • Survey, and HOA documents and dues if you have an HOA
  • Utility costs for the past year

On the Coast

If your home has an elevation certificate, a FORTIFIED roof or a transferable flood policy, say so in the listing. Those can make the home easier and cheaper to insure, and buyers notice.

03

Step 3: Fill out the seller's disclosure

Mississippi's Property Condition Disclosure Statement, answered honestly and completely.

Mississippi law requires most sellers of homes with one to four units to give buyers a Property Condition Disclosure Statement. You fill it out yourself, based on what you know. It asks about the roof, structure, systems, water damage, past flooding from rising water, whether the home is in a FEMA flood hazard zone, whether flood insurance is required and what you pay, and damage from storms.

The law says to give the buyer the disclosure as soon as practicable, before an offer is accepted. If it's delivered later, the buyer has 3 days after it's handed to them (or 5 days after it's mailed) to end the contract by written notice. So it's best to have it done before you list.

Some transfers are exempt, such as court-ordered sales, foreclosures, and transfers between co-owners or to a spouse or children. If you think yours might be exempt, check with a real estate attorney. Homes built before 1978 also need the federal lead-based paint disclosure.

Your agent can give you the form and explain what each question means, but can't answer it for you. When in doubt, disclose.

04

Step 4: Get the house ready

Fix what inspectors and insurers will flag, then make it shine.

Start with the things that can stall a sale: roof leaks, signs of water, plumbing or electrical problems, and an old heating and cooling system. Some sellers get a pre-listing inspection so there are no surprises.

Then focus on first impressions. Declutter, clean, touch up paint, fix small things and tidy the yard. Fresh mulch, a clean porch and good lighting make photos and showings better.

05

Step 5: Price it and go live

The right price, great photos and video, and the MLS.

Pricing right from the start matters. Homes priced well tend to get the most attention in their first couple of weeks. Your agent should show you the comparable sales behind the price.

You'll sign a listing agreement that covers the price, how long the listing lasts, what the agent will do, and how they're paid. Agent pay is negotiable. Then come professional photos, video, the MLS listing and showings.

On the Coast

I shoot drone video along the Coast. Aerial footage shows buyers how close a home is to the water, the harbor or the beach in a way photos can't.

06

Step 6: Compare offers

The highest price isn't always the best offer.

Look at the whole offer: price, type of financing, earnest money, inspection and insurance timelines, closing date, and any requests for help with closing costs or repairs.

Ask your agent for a side-by-side net sheet. An offer with strong financing and a shorter inspection period can be worth more than a slightly higher price.

07

Step 7: Work through inspections

Expect a request list. You have options.

After the buyer's inspections, they may ask for repairs, a credit at closing or a lower price. You can agree, offer something different or say no, within the terms of your contract.

Insurance can come up here too. If a buyer's quote is high because of the roof or a flood zone, your elevation certificate, roof paperwork or a transferable flood policy can help.

08

Step 8: Close the sale

Appraisal, final walk-through, signing day.

The buyer's lender orders an appraisal. If it comes in below the price, the buyer and seller can talk about options depending on the contract.

A real estate attorney or title company handles the closing. Before closing day, leave the home in the agreed condition, and gather keys, garage door openers and any manuals and warranties.

Keep your homeowners and flood insurance in force until the sale has closed. Ask your agent and the closing office before canceling anything. If the buyer is taking over your flood policy, the closing office can help with the transfer.

09

Step 9: After the sale

Keep your closing papers, and talk to a tax professional.

Save your closing statement and records of improvements you made to the home. Many people who sell their main home can exclude some or all of the gain from federal income tax if they meet the rules, but everyone's situation is different. A tax professional can tell you what applies to you.

Update your address with the post office, your bank and your insurance companies, and cancel or transfer your utilities.

This guide is general information about buying and selling homes in Mississippi, last reviewed November 2026. It is not legal, tax or insurance advice, and laws, forms, programs and insurance rules change. For advice about your situation, talk with a Mississippi real estate attorney, a tax professional or a licensed insurance agent.
